opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed a lot, and not in the direction I expected.

When I first went into psychology, I had this romantic picture of it. I thought I'd be studying the mind in a very deep, almost philosophical way: why people feel what they feel, why they make the choices they make. I was drawn to the big questions.

Once I was actually in it, I realized a huge part of the discipline is about method: experimental design, statistics, controlling variables, running studies with fairly small samples and trying to squeeze a clean effect out of very noisy human behavior. That's important work, and I respect it a lot. But I slowly noticed I wasn't getting the excitement I wanted from it. I'd spend months on a study, and at the end the finding would be this small, careful claim about one narrow situation. I kept thinking, "Is this really getting at how the mind works?"

So psychology was where I first learned that I like rigor, but I also need scale. I want to see whether an idea holds up when you push it really hard, with lots of data, lots of computation, something you can actually build and test. That's part of what pulled me toward the more computational side, toward models and systems you can actually run, rather than only describing behavior from the outside.

I don't regret studying it at all. It gave me a way of thinking about cognition, about learning, about how intelligence might be structured, and I still find myself drawing on that intuition. But studying it was also how I found out it wasn't quite the place where I wanted to spend my whole career. I'm grateful I learned that early rather than late.

r001.rationale: Kay says she was drawn to psychology’s big questions and still values what it taught her, but its methods did not excite her and she realized it was not where she wanted to spend her career.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first year almost convinced me I'd made a mistake. I went in thinking psychology was about understanding people, the way you'd understand a close friend. What I got instead was statistics, experimental design, a lot of rats and reaction times. I remember sitting in a cognitive psych lecture thinking, where are the humans?

But something shifted around the second year. I did a research methods course where we had to design our own small study, and I realized the thing I'd found cold was actually the part that fit me. I liked the discipline of it. I liked that you couldn't just assert something about how people work, you had to go find out, and you were usually wrong in an interesting way. That taught me I wasn't really drawn to psychology as empathy. I was drawn to it as a way of being rigorous about messy things.

So it suited me, but not for the reasons I'd expected. The reasons I came in with would have made me a mediocre therapist. The reasons I left with are what I still use every day, which is this habit of asking, okay, but how would we actually know that? I think a lot of people have that experience with their field. You pick it for the story you tell yourself at eighteen, and if you're lucky, it turns out to fit you for something you couldn't have named yet.

r001.rationale: The response says Kay nearly thought she had made a mistake and later found psychology suited her for different reasons, but it does not communicate that she found psychology interesting while feeling personally unsuited to doing it.

astra-6.text: Studying psychology helped me separate my interest in people from my interest in the subject itself. I’d imagined it would mostly be about understanding emotions and behavior, but there was also a lot of research, statistics, and careful questioning of what we think we know. That gave me a more concrete way to ask whether it suited me: did I enjoy the actual work, or just the idea of it? It became less about finding a label for myself and more about noticing what kept me curious.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes interest in people or psychology from enjoying its actual work and questions whether it suited Kay, but it does not clearly state that Kay felt personally unsuited to doing psychology.

sol-6.1.text: Studying psychology helped me separate being interested in a subject from being suited to working in it. I was curious about people and why we behave the way we do, but learning it more systematically made me ask which parts I actually enjoyed and what kind of work I wanted to do. So it became less about deciding, “Is psychology right for me?” and more about understanding where that interest fit into my life.

r001.rationale: The response separates interest in psychology from suitability, but it does not say Kay felt personally unsuited to doing psychology.
